2.text: them, they must keep silent. Here it should be remembered that some cases

3.text: of voluntary death originate in wrath.¹

4.text: I will add here two descriptions of voluntary death noted down from

5.text: information given by the natives. The first one happened in the year 1894,

6.text: on the western Kolyma tundra. The second happened on the same tundra

7.text: a year later. Both were related to me by Aiñanwaˊt.

8.text: “One ᴇlɪˊhɪkɪ had taken a great quantity of goods on credit from a merchant of Yakutsk.

9.text: Several years passed, and the debt was not fully covered. One spring he left his home and went

10.text: to Sredne-Kolymsk from a distant place in the tundra. At the same time all the people passed

11.text: over to the other shore of the Omolon River. His brother was Rultuˊwg̣i. They drank brandy

12.text: there in the tent of Uˊnkuul, a Tungus. A hernia, which was an object of constant care with him,

13.text: was frost-bitten, and therefore refused to go in. Thus ill-luck visited him. He suffered great pain

14.text: and sorrow because he could not put his bowels in place. Therefore he began to speak, requesting

15.text: his companion in marriage to give him death. Uˊnkuul was his companion in marriage. The

16.text: neighboring camp was that of his younger brother. ᴇlɪˊhɪkɪ went to the town with them, without a tent

17.text: of his own. His wife had very small children, (and could not go with them.) Then he was

18.text: afflicted in the manner aforesaid; and, since his father died a voluntary death, he wanted to imitate

20.text: “Oh! why have I not begun with the father first? He was breaking wind badly, and could

21.text: not defecate normally. In his anus was formed a white stone, a soft one, round in form and polished.

22.text: They found it in his rectum after his death. That one asked to be killed. The elder son was

23.text: assisting him. He seemed sighing his last, but unexpectedly tore out the knife and came to life

24.text: again. Since he could not be killed by stabbing, he said, ‘Tighten it on me!’ So they strangled

25.text: him with a rope. When he was dead, they carried him away into the tundra, and, putting his body

26.text: on the ground, investigated his rectum. There they found the white stone. Still when alive, he

27.text: defecated stone or sand, and who knows what not!

28.text: “His son after him came to be in the same position. Therefore, being at the tent of his marriage-

29.text: companion, he asked to be killed. They listened to him, and wanted to obey him. In obedience

30.text: to him, they put him on a grated sled and took him to his brother’s tent. There they executed his

31.text: desire. The younger brother was assisting him, but he could not do it in a proper way. His hand

32.text: trembled. He himself said, ‘There, turn the knife a little more aside;’ but his assistant could not

33.text: do it. Then he used that very word of his father,² ‘Tighten it on me!’ Indeed, they strangled him

34.text: with a rope and killed him. That was the end.”

35.text: Another story refers to a desire for voluntary death once expressed and

36.text: then revoked. The story is as follows: —

37.text: “My neighbor in the camp, Little-Spoon by name, also asked to be killed. With many words

38.text: he persuaded his house-mates. Before that, he had quarrelled with his wife. They had very bad

39.text: sons. His sons and their mother quarrelled with their father. For that reason he was angered.

40.text: Therefore he asked to be killed. They had only driving-reindeer, almost no other reindeer. The

41.text: other sons slaughtered a woman’s driving-reindeer led by the halter (i. e., very well broken), because

42.text: he had many more sons. But the oldest son quarrelled with him. Therefore it was necessary to

43.text: kill a reindeer-buck for his last meal. We thought he was really asking to be killed. We made

44.text: haste and prepared everything necessary. We replaced the broken and mended parts of the sledges

45.text: ¹ According to Jochelson (The Koryak, p. 760), the custom of killing old people, until recently, existed

46.text: among the Koryak. Franz Boas says of the Central Eskimo, that among them it is considered lawful for a man

47.text: to kill his aged parents (Boas, Central Eskimo, p. 615).
